title: Construction Dust & Silica
whatItIs: Cutting, drilling, grinding and sanding make fine dust that damages the lungs. The three main types are silica dust, wood dust and general dust, such as gypsum from plasterboard.
keyFacts: Silica dust comes from concrete, mortar, sandstone, bricks and tiles. The finest dust is too fine to see.
Dust causes lung cancer, silicosis, COPD and asthma. Silica is believed to kill over 500 construction workers a year.

keyFacts.text: COSHH applies to construction dust: employers MUST prevent exposure or adequately control it.

keyFacts: First stop or reduce the dust: right-size materials, or a block splitter instead of a cut-off saw.
Then stop dust getting into the air: water suppression or on-tool extraction.
RPE is the last line of protection. The general level for construction dust is APF 20.

visual.caption: Controls for common high-risk dust tasks (HSE CIS36)

notes: APF 20: e.g. an FFP3 disposable mask, or a half mask with a P3 filter.

a.label: Water suppression
points: Damps down dust clouds as you cut
Needs enough water for the whole time you work

b.label: On-tool extraction
points: Removes dust at the tool as it's made
Needs an H, M or L class unit, not a general vacuum
Examined and tested at least every 14 months

onTheTest.question: You're cutting kerbs with a cut-off saw. Which controls does HSE guidance give?
options: Wet the kerb once before cutting
Cut quickly so there's less dust
Water suppression plus RPE with an APF of 20
Work outdoors, so no controls are needed
onTheTest.why: HSE CIS36 Table 1: cutting kerbs, blocks and paving with a cut-off saw needs water suppression plus RPE with an APF of 20.

onTheTest.question: Why must someone wearing a tight-fitting dust mask be clean-shaven?
options: Stubble or a beard stops the mask sealing to the face
It's a site dress code rule
It makes the face fit test quicker
onTheTest.why: HSG150: respirators don't seal well against a beard. CIS36: tight-fitting masks need face fit testing and a clean-shaven wearer.

traps: Just wetting the material first doesn't work: water is needed for the whole time you cut.
Working outside doesn't make it safe: high-energy tools still make a lot of dust.
Damage builds up slowly: by the time you notice, it may be serious.
Don't rely on a mask alone: RPE is the last line of protection.
